selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about how modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect performance. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline with no aggregation or fusion, so later experiments can each change one factor against it: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile avgpool or transformer aggregation, image-only models, or adding a second modality. 3) Under a limited budget, a clean baseline is the most efficient first step. It gives later comparisons a clear interpretation and avoids starting with a complex multimodal setup whose result we could not attribute to any single design choice.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: We have only one result. The single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline reached 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. We know nothing yet about how informative the image modality is, and that question decides whether most of the remaining space (image-only and multimodal configurations) is worth exploring. 2. What this tests: The matched single-profile, image-only ResNet50 baseline. It changes only the modality relative to config_001, with no aggregation or fusion, so it gives a clean comparison of RNA versus image signal. 3. Why now: Testing modality first is the highest-value way to reduce uncertainty. If images are weak, the budget can focus on RNA encoders and profile settings. If images are competitive or complementary, fusion experiments become well motivated. Profile setting and encoder choice can be isolated in later one-variable experiments.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only with PCA on a single profile (0.536 accuracy, 0.516 F1) far outperforms image-only with ResNet50 (0.227 accuracy, 0.191 F1). RNA therefore looks like the stronger base modality. We still know nothing about whether combining multiple profiles helps, and that choice affects most of the remaining search space. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the best-known setup (RNA-only, PCA n2000) and changes only one thing, single profile to multiprofile with simple average pooling. Any change in accuracy or F1 can then be attributed to the profile setting. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it builds on the strongest result so far while answering a broad design question in a clean way. If multiprofile helps, the next steps would be transformer aggregation and the multiprofile multimodal variants. If it does not, we can deprioritize much of the multiprofile space. Changing the encoder or adding fusion now would answer a narrower question or vary several choices at once.

Evidence: RNA clearly outperforms image (0.536 vs 0.227 accuracy in single-profile). Switching RNA from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.536 to 0.688 accuracy, F1 0.516 to 0.659), so multiprofile RNA is the strongest direction so far. Aggregation is still untested beyond avgpool. This experiment keeps the best configuration (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only avgpool to transformer, which isolates the effect of the aggregation method. That makes it a cheap, clean exploitation step. Its result will tell us which aggregation to carry into later encoder and multimodal comparisons, so it is a good use of the limited budget before those choices multiply the search space.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool on pca_n2000 (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). It clearly beats single-profile (0.536) and transformer aggregation (0.512). Image-only resnet50 is weak (0.227), so adding images may not help much. The RNA encoder is still completely untested: every RNA result so far uses pca_n2000. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scvi_n200. This isolates whether a learned latent representation beats PCA features under the winning aggregation. 3. Why now: The encoder choice affects every RNA and multimodal configuration remaining, so resolving it early guides most of the rest of the search. It is also a strong exploitation candidate, since it extends the best known setup and could improve on it directly.

Evidence: multiprofile avgpool clearly beats singleprofile for RNA (0.688 vs 0.536 with PCA). Transformer aggregation underperformed with PCA (0.512). PCA edged out scVI under avgpool (0.688 vs 0.635). ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.227 singleprofile). The largest untested axis is multimodal fusion, which covers most of the remaining search space. We do not yet know whether image features add complementary signal or only add noise. This experiment adds ResNet50 images to the best known setup (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) using simple concat fusion, changing a single factor relative to config_002. If it beats 0.688, the multimodal branch is worth exploring further, including weighted fusion and ViT-L. If it does not, we can deprioritize much of the multimodal space and spend the remaining budget on RNA encoders such as scGPT. That makes it the most uncertainty-reducing experiment for the budget.

1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal so far. Multiprofile with avgpool clearly beat singleprofile (0.688 vs 0.536 accuracy). Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.512). Within the avgpool setting, PCA beat scVI (0.688 vs 0.635), and F1 agrees. ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.227), and adding it by concat fusion lowered performance to 0.532. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is still untested in the strongest setting. 2) This experiment changes only the RNA encoder from the current best (config_002), swapping PCA for scGPT while keeping multiprofile and avgpool. It completes the encoder comparison and shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats PCA. 3) This is a clean one-factor test on the strongest RNA-only setting, so it can either produce a new best model or confirm that PCA is the right RNA backbone. Either result guides later multimodal tests. Those would more sensibly try weighted fusion or the ViT-L image encoder on top of the best RNA encoder, rather than spend more budget on combinations that keep the weak image branch now.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002, accuracy 0.688). Adding ResNet50 images through concat fusion (config_018) dropped accuracy to 0.532. ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.227). It is unclear whether multimodal fails because image features carry little signal or because naive concatenation lets noisy image features dilute the strong RNA signal. 2. Test: config_019 differs from config_018 only in fusion (weighted instead of concat), with RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting and aggregation held fixed. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers or beats config_002, fusion design is the bottleneck and multimodal remains worth exploring. If it stays near 0.53 or below, ResNet50 image features likely hurt regardless of fusion, which argues for trying ViT-L or focusing on RNA-only. 3. Why now: with a limited budget, this one controlled comparison decides whether the large multimodal part of the search space deserves further experiments, while staying anchored to the best-performing RNA setup.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.688). Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile and transformer aggregation. Multimodal weighted fusion with ResNet50 (config_019, 0.650) came close but did not surpass it, and it clearly beat concat fusion (config_018, 0.532). Image-only ResNet50 was very weak (0.227), so the weak image representation is a plausible reason fusion has not added value. The ViT-L image encoder is completely untested. 2) Test: config_025 changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) relative to config_019, keeping PCA, multiprofile, avgpool and weighted fusion fixed. This isolates whether a stronger image representation lets multimodal fusion beat the RNA-only best. 3) Why now: it resolves the main open question, whether imaging can add value at all, using the best-established settings for the other factors. It has a real chance of improving on the current best, and if it fails, that is strong evidence to focus the remaining budget on RNA-only refinements.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.688). Within multimodal runs, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.650 vs 0.532 with PCA+ResNet50), but adding images has not yet beaten the RNA-only baseline. With PCA, it lowered accuracy from 0.688 to 0.650. Two things remain unclear: whether the weighted-fusion advantage is general, and whether images ever add value to RNA. 2. What this tests: config_031 adds ResNet50 images with weighted fusion to the scVI multiprofile avgpool model (config_005, acc 0.635). That is a single-change comparison against config_005, isolating whether images help an scVI RNA branch. It also differs from config_019 only in the RNA encoder, which shows whether the weighted-fusion gain carries over across RNA encoders. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: It reuses the strongest known settings (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and has a realistic chance of a competitive score. It also directly reduces uncertainty about the central question of whether multimodal fusion beats RNA-only. Each outcome is informative: a gain over 0.635 would support pursuing fusion further, while a drop would strengthen the case for RNA-only modeling.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. The single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.494 accuracy and 0.453 F1. We have no information yet on how useful the image modality is, so the most basic axis of the design space is still unexplored. 2. Evidence: two single-profile unimodal baselines are done. RNA (PCA) reached 0.494 accuracy / 0.453 F1, and image (ResNet50) reached 0.411 / 0.378. RNA looks stronger, but it is still unknown whether the two modalities carry complementary information. The other major choices (profile setting, encoder, fusion) are also untested. Test: config_016 is a single-profile multimodal model that concatenates exactly the two encoders already tested. It differs from both baselines only by combining them, so any gain or loss isolates the value of multimodality without confounding from encoder or profile changes. Why now: whether to fuse modalities is the most consequential branching decision in this search space, since most remaining configurations are multimodal. Answering it cleanly with the simplest fusion method (concat) tells us whether to spend later experiments on fusion, aggregation and encoder variants within multimodal models, or to focus on RNA-only refinements such as scVI/scGPT encoders and multiprofile aggregation.

1. Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001, acc 0.494, F1 0.453) is the strongest result so far. Image-only ResNet50 is lower (0.411). Multimodal concat (0.260) is far below both unimodal baselines, so naive fusion is currently hurting performance. Profile setting and aggregation have not been tested at all. 2. Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, on the best-performing RNA-only PCA baseline. This isolates whether multiprofile input helps. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a major design axis that applies across most of the remaining configurations. Testing it on the strongest and simplest branch builds on the best evidence so far while answering an open question. The multimodal failure is worth revisiting with weighted fusion later, but that branch looks less promising right now.

Evidence: RNA-only is the strongest modality (0.494 single-profile, 0.519 multiprofile avgpool). Image-only is weaker (0.411). Concat multimodal fusion collapsed to 0.260 accuracy and 0.222 F1, well below either unimodal model. That points to a fusion failure rather than a lack of complementary signal, but one run cannot show whether the failure comes from concat itself or from multimodal fusion in general. Test: config_017 is identical to config_016 except that it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, so it isolates the fusion choice. Why now: most of the remaining space (about 35 configurations) is multimodal. If weighted fusion recovers to at least RNA-only level, multimodal stays a viable direction. If it also collapses, we can deprioritize multimodal configurations and spend the remaining budget on RNA encoder and aggregation choices. This single-variable experiment resolves the largest current uncertainty in the search space.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is the strongest modality so far (RNA-only single-profile 0.494 vs image-only 0.411). Multiprofile avgpool gave a modest gain (0.519 accuracy, 0.480 F1), which is the current best. Multimodal fusion has not beaten RNA-only: concat collapsed to 0.260 and weighted reached 0.435. The RNA encoder choice is completely untested, since every run so far used pca_n2000, even though it may be one of the most influential design decisions. 2) What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, while keeping the best setting fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the encoder effect in the best-performing context. 3) Why it is the best next step: it combines exploitation (it builds on the current best) with exploration (it answers an open, high-impact question). Its result will tell us whether later multimodal and aggregation experiments should keep PCA or switch to the scVI encoder.

1. Evidence: In RNA-only multiprofile models with avgpool, switching the encoder from PCA to scVI raised accuracy from 0.519 to 0.650, with a matching F1 gain from 0.480 to 0.628. This is the largest effect seen so far. Multiprofile beat singleprofile only modestly with PCA (0.519 vs 0.494). Multimodal fusion has not beaten RNA-only, and weighted fusion clearly outperformed concat. Transformer aggregation has never been tested, so the aggregation choice is the main open question. 2. Test: config_006 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates the aggregation effect on the strongest backbone. 3. Why now: It is both exploitation and exploration. It could improve on the current best result. It also settles whether learned aggregation is worth carrying into later multiprofile and multimodal configurations, which affects many remaining candidates. Testing scGPT (config_008) is a close alternative but can follow next.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest lever seen so far. Within RNA-only multiprofile avgpool, scVI (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) beat PCA (0.519 acc, 0.480 F1). Avgpool clearly beat the transformer aggregator for scVI (0.224). Multimodal fusion has not yet beaten RNA-only (best fused result 0.435 with weighted fusion). The third RNA encoder, scGPT, is completely untested. 2) Test: config_008 keeps the best-performing setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder to scGPT. This isolates the effect of the foundation-model representation against scVI and PCA. 3) Value: The encoder choice affects every later RNA-only and multimodal configuration. Settling it now, with a clean one-factor comparison, tells us which RNA backbone to carry into fusion experiments. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. Adding images to scVI is a natural next step but rests on weaker evidence, since fusion has so far hurt performance.

1. Evidence: The clearest signal so far is the RNA encoder. scVI multiprofile with avgpool (config_005) reached 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1, well above PCA (0.519) and scGPT (0.227) under the same setting. The transformer aggregator performed poorly (0.224), so avgpool is the safer choice. Multimodal results are mixed. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat in singleprofile (0.435 vs 0.260), but both still trailed RNA-only, and the image-only ResNet50 baseline was weaker (0.411). The open question is whether images add anything once a strong RNA representation is used. 2. Test: config_031 keeps config_005's choices fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes one thing: it adds ResNet50 image features with weighted fusion, the better-performing fusion method. This directly measures the marginal value of the image modality on top of the best RNA setup. 3. Why now: This exploits the strongest finding and answers the central question of whether to fuse modalities, using a single-variable comparison. If it beats 0.650, multimodal fusion becomes the direction to pursue (for example, trying the ViT image encoder next). If it does not, the budget can shift to refining RNA-only models, such as testing scVI singleprofile to isolate the profile effect.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.653 accuracy. It barely beats RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, 0.650). Validation F1 is nearly identical for the two. So with ResNet50, the image branch adds little. ResNet50 image-only results are also weak (0.41). The image encoder choice is the largest untested factor: imagenet_vit_l has never been tried. 2) Test: config_037 keeps every setting of the best configuration and swaps only ResNet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the image encoder effect in the strongest setup. If accuracy rises clearly above about 0.65, image representation quality was what limited the multimodal gain. If it does not, the image modality likely contributes little, and later experiments should focus on RNA, aggregation and fusion. 3) Why now: it is a one-variable change from the current best, so it could improve the top result while also resolving a major open question. Under a limited budget, that makes it more useful than re-checking fusion type or the transformer aggregation, which has already performed poorly.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. What it tests: config_001 is the simplest setup: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components), with no aggregation or fusion. It gives a low-complexity reference point. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: a learned RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool or transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion. 3. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment has been run. RNA-only, single-profile, PCA reached 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. We have no information yet about the image modality, which half of the search space depends on. 2. What this tests: image-only, single-profile ResNet50 keeps the simplest setting (single profile, no aggregation, no fusion) and swaps only the modality. Compared with config_001, it gives a clean RNA-versus-image baseline. It shows whether images carry predictive signal alone and how strong that signal is relative to RNA. 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: whether images are informative is the main question behind all the multimodal and image configurations. If image-only performs poorly, multimodal configurations become lower priority and budget can go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it performs comparably or better, fusion experiments are well motivated. ResNet50 is the cheaper, standard image encoder, so it is a sensible first image baseline before testing ViT-L.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: There are only two single-profile baselines. Image-only ResNet50 (acc 0.721, F1 0.681) beat RNA-only PCA (acc 0.650, F1 0.628). This shows each modality alone carries useful signal. It does not show whether the two are complementary. That is the most important open design question, because it decides whether the large multimodal half of the search space is worth exploring. 2. What this tests: config_016 combines exactly the two tested encoders (PCA RNA + ResNet50 image) with the simplest fusion (concat), still in the single-profile setting. Representation, profile setting and aggregation stay fixed, so any gain or loss over 0.721 can be attributed to adding RNA through fusion. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: If fusion clearly helps, later budget can go to multimodal variants such as weighted fusion, other encoders and multiprofile. If it does not, the search can focus on image-only refinements such as ViT-L or multiprofile aggregation. Either result cuts uncertainty across most of the remaining configurations.

1. Evidence: image-only ResNet50 is the best so far (acc 0.721, F1 0.681), ahead of RNA-only PCA (0.650). Multimodal PCA+ResNet50 with concat fusion scored only 0.527, below both single-modality models. That suggests the fusion step itself may be failing, but one run cannot tell us whether multimodal models are inherently weak here or concat is a poor fusion choice. 2. Test: config_017 keeps everything identical to config_016 (single-profile, PCA, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion to weighted. This isolates the fusion method. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above image-only, concat is the problem. If it also underperforms, multimodal fusion is broadly unhelpful in this setup. 3. Why now: about two-thirds of the remaining configurations are multimodal, and every one depends on this fusion choice. A single controlled comparison tells us whether to deprioritize concat, deprioritize multimodal models altogether, or keep exploring them. That makes it a better use of the budget than immediately exploiting the image-only direction (e.g., multiprofile or ViT-L image-only), which can follow next.

1) Evidence: the image_only ResNet50 single-profile model is the best so far (acc 0.721, F1 0.681). It beats RNA-only PCA (0.650), and both multimodal fusions scored worse (concat 0.527, weighted 0.579). This suggests fusion is not helping, at least with the current encoders. The profile setting, however, is completely untested, since every run so far used a single profile. 2) This experiment changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), while keeping the strongest modality and encoder fixed. 1) Evidence: image-only ResNet50 singleprofile (config_010) is the best result so far, at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. It beats RNA-only PCA (0.650). Both multimodal fusions with these encoders scored worse (0.527 and 0.579), and multiprofile avgpool dropped image performance sharply (0.421). 1. Evidence: Single-profile ResNet50 image-only is the best result so far (acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Moving to multiprofile with avgpool caused a large drop (0.421). It is unclear whether that drop comes from multiprofile itself or from avgpool, which may wash out profile-specific signal. Multimodal fusion and ViT-L have also underperformed, so the strongest components so far are ResNet50 and single-profile input. 2. Test: Config_012 keeps everything from config_011 (image-only, ResNet50, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregation to a transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. If accuracy recovers to near or above 0.72, learned aggregation can make multiprofile useful. If it stays low, multiprofile is likely harmful in this setting, and many remaining multiprofile configurations can be deprioritized. 3. Why now: The multiprofile/aggregation question affects most of the remaining search space. Testing it on the strongest encoder, with a single-variable change, gives the most decision-relevant information per experiment. RNA encoder alternatives (scVI, scGPT) remain an important next question.

Evidence: the best result so far is single-profile image_only with resnet50 (0.721 acc, 0.681 F1), followed by RNA-only with pca_n2000 (0.650). Both multimodal fusions with pca_n2000 and resnet50 did worse than either unimodal model (0.527 and 0.579). For multiprofile, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.632 vs 0.421), but it still did not beat single-profile. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L hurt badly (0.411). The biggest untested design choice is the RNA representation: every RNA result so far, unimodal and multimodal, used high-dimensional PCA. That PCA input may also explain the poor fusion results. This experiment swaps pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 in the simplest setting (RNA-only, single-profile) and changes nothing else, so it isolates the RNA encoder effect against config_001. A direct comparison of this kind is the cheapest way to learn whether a learned, low-dimensional RNA latent improves RNA performance. If it does, it gives a principled reason to revisit multimodal fusion with scvi. If it does not, the remaining budget can go to image-centric and aggregation refinements instead of more multimodal combinations that blindly reuse PCA.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the single-profile ResNet50 image-only model (acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Both PCA+ResNet50 multimodal runs score well below either unimodal baseline: concat 0.527 and weighted 0.579. So fusion currently hurts, though weighted fusion does better than concat. On their own, scVI (0.635) and PCA (0.650) perform about the same in RNA-only. Multiprofile has not helped ResNet50 so far: avgpool 0.421, transformer 0.632. 2. Test: This run keeps the better-performing setup fixed (single-profile, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It asks whether the multimodal drop comes from the PCA representation, for example a noisy, high-dimensional RNA input that disrupts fusion, or from fusing modalities in this setting in general. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion can help at all is the biggest open question and controls most of the remaining search space (30+ multimodal configs). A one-variable comparison against config_017 answers it directly. If scVI fusion recovers to or above the image-only baseline, multimodal configs with compact RNA encoders are worth exploring. If it stays low, evidence that fusion is the problem gets stronger, and the remaining budget should shift toward unimodal and encoder questions such as scGPT.

It therefore measures the quality of scGPT embeddings directly, without confounds from fusion or aggregation. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It is a cheap, clean comparison on the largest unexplored design axis. A strong scGPT result would make scGPT plus ResNet50 weighted fusion (config_041) a well-motivated next step. A weak result would let us drop a large share of the remaining space and focus the budget on scVI and ResNet50 extensions.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. 1. Evidence: The two strongest unimodal models are close: ImageNet ViT-L single-profile image (0.725 acc) and PCA single-profile RNA (0.721 acc). Multiprofile aggregation has so far hurt RNA performance, so single-profile is the stronger base. 2. Test: config_023 changes only the fusion method, concat to weighted, from config_022. 1) Evidence: The image encoder is the clearest driver so far. Switching from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l raised accuracy from 0.629 to 0.713. Concat fusion beat weighted (0.725 vs 0.635). 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. 1. Evidence: All three single-profile baselines sit in a narrow band (0.519–0.532 accuracy). Image-only ResNet50 is slightly ahead and has a clearly higher F1 (0.516 vs about 0.48). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA encoder choice has the largest effect seen so far among working encoders. By contrast, profile setting and aggregation look like small effects: on image-only resnet50, multiprofile scored 0.523 with avgpool and 0.514 with transformer, versus 0.532 single-profile. What this tests: scGPT RNA-only in the single-profile setting gives a clean, one-variable comparison against config_001 (PCA) and config_004 (scVI). Why this is the best next experiment: The result determines which RNA encoder should go into later multiprofile and multimodal runs. If scGPT beats PCA, a whole block of scGPT configurations becomes worth exploiting. If not, those configurations can be deprioritized and the remaining budget focused on PCA with resnet50 variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: scGPT RNA-only (config_007) is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.586, F1 0.574). It beats PCA (0.519) and scVI (0.427) by a wide margin, so RNA representation is the strongest design lever observed. Fusion evidence comes only from the PCA encoder. With PCA, concat fusion (0.520) matched RNA-only but did not improve on it and fell slightly below ResNet50 image-only (0.532). Weighted fusion hurt badly (0.435). Multiprofile aggregation has not helped image-only ResNet50 (avgpool 0.523, transformer 0.514, vs single-profile 0.532). So it is unclear whether adding images helps once a strong RNA encoder is used. 2. What this tests: config_040 adds ResNet50 image features to scGPT with concat fusion in the single-profile setting. This is a single-factor extension of the best configuration. It keeps the best RNA encoder, the better image encoder (ViT-L was poor), the better-performing fusion type and the better-performing profile setting. It isolates whether the image modality adds complementary signal to strong RNA embeddings. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: it exploits the strongest signal while answering a key open question about multimodal value. If it beats 0.586, the multimodal scGPT branch is worth exploring further. If it does not, the search can focus on scGPT RNA-only variants such as multiprofile aggregation, and avoid spending budget on many multimodal configurations.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only single-profile baseline with PCA (config_001) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Evidence: we have only two single-profile baselines. RNA (PCA) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Image (ResNet50) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. RNA looks stronger, but with one run each this gap is not conclusive. The biggest open question is whether the two modalities carry complementary information. Test: config_016 combines exactly the two already-tested encoders (PCA plus ResNet50, single-profile) with the simplest fusion (concat). Any change from the unimodal baselines can therefore be attributed to adding the second modality, not to a new encoder or to aggregation. Why now: the result determines whether the large multimodal part of the search space (most remaining configs) deserves the budget, or whether effort should go to RNA-only encoder and multiprofile variants. If concat beats RNA-only, weighted fusion and multiprofile extensions become logical next steps. If not, we can deprioritize multimodal configurations early.

1) Evidence: RNA-only with PCA reached 0.678 accuracy and image-only with ResNet50 reached 0.619. Concat fusion of those same two encoders collapsed to 0.224 accuracy and 0.184 F1, far below either single modality. That points to a failure in the fusion step, such as feature-scale imbalance or optimization trouble with concatenation, rather than a lack of useful signal. 2) This experiment keeps the encoders (PCA-2000 and ResNet50) and the single-profile setting fixed and swaps only concat for weighted fusion, so any change can be attributed to the fusion method. 3) Most of the remaining space is multimodal. Learning early whether weighted fusion recovers or beats the unimodal baselines, or whether multimodal models fail regardless of fusion, decides whether to keep investing there or turn to encoder and multiprofile exploration of the stronger RNA-only branch.

1. Evidence: The strongest result so far is the simplest model, RNA-only PCA single-profile (acc 0.678, F1 0.646). Image-only is weaker (0.619). Multimodal fusion has not beaten RNA-only: weighted fusion reached 0.635, and concat collapsed to 0.224, which suggests concat is fragile or unstable here. Every completed run is single-profile, so the effect of multiprofile aggregation is entirely unknown. That axis touches about two-thirds of the remaining configurations. 2. Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregator (avgpool), on the best-performing RNA-only PCA baseline. Why now: Profile setting and aggregation is the largest unresolved design question. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only singleprofile with PCA is the best result so far (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). It beats image-only ResNet50 (0.619) and weighted multimodal fusion (0.635). Multimodal fusion has not beaten RNA-only: weighted fusion reached 0.635 and concat collapsed to 0.224. For example, swapping in scVI or scGPT isolates the encoder, adding multiprofile with avgpool or a transformer isolates profile setting and aggregation, and adding an image encoder with concat or weighted fusion isolates the value of multimodality. 3. Why now: starting with a complex multimodal, multiprofile model would mix several factors together, so we could not tell which one drove the result. This baseline is cheap, low-variance and directly informative. It anchors the search and shows whether more complex models are actually worth their cost.

1) Evidence so far: there is only one result, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.328, F1 0.288).
